Remove detections isolated in time

Source: R/filter_lag.R
filter_min_lag.Rd

A false detection, from two transmissions that collide, is rarely followed by the same code on the same receiver soon after. For each detection the minimum lag is the shorter of two times: back to the previous detection and forward to the next, both of its own transmitter on its own receiver. A detection with no other of its transmitter on its receiver has none. The filter keeps detections whose minimum lag lies between min_lag_s and max_lag_s, inclusive. With min_lag_s = 0 it keeps the same rows as false_detections(det, tf = max_lag_s) in the glatos package when glatos computes the lags itself. A GLATOS export carries a min_lag column computed on the server, which false_detections() uses when present; it can differ from the lags of the rows in hand (1 of 5,923 lamprey rows in the glatos example), so drop that column before comparing.

Usage

filter_min_lag(x, max_lag_s, min_lag_s = 0, long_lag_s = NULL)

Arguments

x

A detset().

max_lag_s

Longest minimum lag kept, in seconds.

min_lag_s

Shortest minimum lag kept, in seconds. Above 0 it also removes detections closer together than any tag transmits.

long_lag_s

Optional interval, in seconds, above which an interval is long. NULL, the default, leaves the second condition off. It must exceed max_lag_s.

Value

x with the detections kept and one log record, with the reasons isolated (minimum lag above max_lag_s, or none), too_close and, with long_lag_s, few_short_intervals; the record then also counts the transmitter and receiver pairs tested and those that failed.

Details

Pincock (2012) suggests a short interval of 30 times the average delay of the tags as max_lag_s; detqc takes the average delay as the mean of each tag's minimum and maximum delay. The threshold is a choice the analysis must state. minimum_lags() returns the lags this filter tests, so their distribution can inform it.

Pincock's test has two conditions: at least one short interval, and more short intervals than long ones. By default this filter applies only the first, as glatos does. long_lag_s adds the second; Pincock suggests 720 times the average delay, 24 times max_lag_s when that is 30 times the delay. The note does not say over which detections or which period the intervals are counted. Here they are counted for each transmitter on each receiver, over all of its detections in the set when the filter runs: an interval is the time between two consecutive detections of the pair, it is short from min_lag_s to max_lag_s inclusive, and long above long_lag_s. A pair with no more short intervals than long ones fails, and every detection of that transmitter on that receiver is removed, with the reason few_short_intervals where the first condition kept it. The test catches a code heard now and then over a long record, as a false code that repeats or a tag at the edge of a receiver's range for weeks, when it is heard alone between its close pairs. Where every gap between visits is long, n close pairs give n short intervals and n - 1 long ones, so a code heard only in close pairs passes however rare. With max_lag_s = 3600 and long_lag_s = 86400, four close pairs, 60 s apart within a pair and 3 days apart between pairs, give 4 short intervals against 3 long, and all 8 detections stay. Each lone detection between the pairs adds a long interval when both of its gaps exceed long_lag_s: one lone detection midway between two pairs, 1.5 days from each, makes a tie, 4 against 4, and all 9 detections go. The test does not look across receivers, so it cannot tell a real visit of a few detections from a false one. It also does not read the receiver's own statistics, which Pincock uses for a second scan of the detections the first scan rejects.

References

Pincock, D. G. (2012). False detections: what they are and how to remove them from detection data. Application note DOC-004691-03, Amirix Systems Inc. (VEMCO).

See also

Other filters: filter_animals(), filter_deployment_period(), filter_duplicates(), filter_min_detections(), filter_post_release(), filter_release(), filter_speed(), filter_tag_life(), minimum_lags()

Examples

study <- detqc_example
dets <- detset(study$detections, study$deployments, study$animals)
dets <- filter_min_lag(dets, max_lag_s = 3600)
writeLines(strwrap(detset_log(dets)$reason[2], width = 72))
#> removed 51 of 3,297 detections (1.55%); 0 animals lost every detection
# Add Pincock's second condition: more short intervals than long ones
both <- filter_min_lag(dets, max_lag_s = 3600, long_lag_s = 24 * 3600)
writeLines(strwrap(detset_log(both)$reason[3], width = 72))
#> removed 0 of 3,246 detections (0%); 0 animals lost every detection; 0
#> of 32 transmitter and receiver pairs had no more short intervals than
#> long
